During the intense trade war between Trump and China, tariffs were announced almost every week, and companies like Logitech immediately raised the prices of their products in the US market significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled that these tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. However, there is still no indication that the relevant companies will pass the refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is currently underway to try to correct this situation...

Trump's tariff storm

Last year, Trump seized on the large US trade deficit with China, apparently believing that imposing hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the US.

Of course, that was never a realistic possibility. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, specialised expertise, and cheap labour needed to produce consumer electronics on such a scale.

Trump has always insisted that China pays the tariffs, but in reality, the tariffs are borne by US brands importing finished goods, and these added costs are ultimately passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At its most absurd point, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that tariffs already paid must be returned to US businesses. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that this cost was ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and there is currently no sign that any of the affected companies intend to refund their customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech over this, seeking to recover refunds for consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

The principle of this matter is beyond dispute. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding them. Morally speaking, they should return that portion to consumers who purchased products during that period.

However, putting this into practice is extremely difficult. Logitech would need to identify all relevant transactions across its vast network of third-party retailers, record the prices consumers paid, and calculate the proportion of those increases attributable to tariffs.

If this lawsuit succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it's worth noting that in class-action suits, the only ones who truly profit are usually the lawyers, while the average payout consumers ultimately receive is typically very low.
